title: Quantization-Aware Healing: Distill, Don't Re-fit
hook: Compress a 120B to 60B, drop it to 4 bits, and it breaks. QAT heals it slowly and then collapses; distilling from the original model instead gets there ~7x faster and stays stable.
key_points: Shipping cheap LLMs now means both structural compression and 4-bit quantization — together they degrade reasoning, math, code, and long context.
The default recovery, quantization-aware training, re-fits the compressed model to hard labels; the authors saw slow convergence and a collapse past peak.
Key insight: a structurally compressed model's bfloat16 checkpoint is itself only a distillation-recovered approximation, not a real full-precision model.
QAH therefore distills the 4-bit student directly from the original uncompressed teacher instead of re-fitting to labels.
On a GPT-OSS 120B to 60B to MXFP4 pipeline, the student matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks at roughly 4x less weight memory.
It reaches a comparable peak about 7x faster than matched QAT and stays stable under continued training, with no hand-tuned early stopping.
content_html: Serving a large model cheaply increasingly means two compressions stacked on each other: cut the parameter count structurally, then quantize what's left to 4 bits. Both hurt, and together they hurt enough — on reasoning, math, coding, and long-context behaviour — that you need a recovery, or healing, stage before shipping. Ryskulov and colleagues report that the standard recovery, quantization-aware training, behaved badly in their pipeline: slow to converge, then collapsing once past its peak.
extra_html:
The teacher you actually want

Their fix rests on a neat observation. A structurally compressed model was never trained at full precision in its own right — its bfloat16 checkpoint is itself a distillation-recovered approximation of the original network. So re-fitting the 4-bit student to that checkpoint's hard labels means learning from a copy of a copy. Quantization-Aware Healing instead distills the 4-bit student directly from the original, uncompressed model.

Results and caveats

Running a GPT-OSS 120B to 60B to MXFP4 pipeline, the authors report the QAH student matching or beating its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks at roughly a quarter of the weight memory and half the teacher's parameter count, released open-weight as Hypernova-60B. Against a matched QAT baseline it reaches a comparable peak about 7x faster and does not degrade under continued training. They also flag a deployment lesson worth remembering: a large, reproducible quality gap between distributed-training backends.

related.hook: Liquid AI distilled BF16 teachers straight into Q4_0 students and recovered 97% of the accuracy that post-training quantization was throwing away.

related.title: Gemma 4 QAT: 4-Bit Weights That Keep Their Quality
related.hook: Squeezing a model to 4 bits after training loses quality. Quantization-aware training bakes the rounding into training instead — and Google shipped Gemma 4 checkpoints that do exactly that.

related.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
related.hook: A big model's softened probabilities say more than hard labels - they reveal how classes relate, so training a small model to mimic them transfers knowledge a one-hot target never could.

flashcards.prompt: Why does QAH distill from the original uncompressed model rather than the compressed bfloat16 checkpoint?
flashcards.back_html: A structurally compressed model was never independently trained at full precision — its bfloat16 checkpoint is already a distillation-recovered approximation, so the original model is the better teacher.

flashcards.prompt: What went wrong with quantization-aware training in the authors' pipeline?

choices.text: It converged slowly and then collapsed past its peak, needing hand-tuned early stopping
It required more weight memory than the uncompressed model
It could not represent 4-bit weights at all
It only worked on models under 10B parameters

flashcards.explanation_html: QAT re-fits the compressed, quantized model to hard labels; in this pipeline that was both slow and unstable, which is what motivated the distillation-based alternative.

flashcards.prompt: What surprising result does the QAH student achieve?
flashcards.back_html: On a GPT-OSS 120B to 60B to MXFP4 pipeline it matches or beats its own bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, at roughly 4x less weight memory and half the teacher's parameters.
